sourceCheck:
Checked on 2026-10-08. Pin: CSS behavior defined by the cited CSSWG specifications and supported MDN features, with no single CSS version number. CSS Snapshot 2026 (https://www.w3.org/TR/css-2026/) is a W3C Group Note dated 22 June 2026. Section 2.1 gives the official definition; 2.2 lists reliable Candidate Recommendations, including Cascade 5, Grid 2 and Media Queries 4. Display 3 is actually in 2.3, the fairly stable group with limited implementation experience. Section 2.4 lists modules with rough interoperability, including Transitions, Animations 1, Sizing 3, Logical Properties 1, Positioned Layout 3, Color 5, Selectors 4 and Nesting 1.
Specification headers read: css-cascade-5: Candidate Recommendation Snapshot, 13 January 2022; css-cascade-6: Working Draft, 6 September 2024; selectors-4 TR: Working Draft, 22 January 2026; selectors-4 editor's draft: Editor's Draft, 18 September 2026; css-nesting-1: Working Draft, 22 January 2026; css-values-4: Working Draft, 12 March 2024; css-variables-1: Candidate Recommendation Snapshot, 16 June 2022; css-properties-values-api-1: Working Draft, 26 March 2024; css-box-3: Recommendation, 11 April 2024; css-sizing-3: Working Draft, 4 September 2026; css-display-3: Candidate Recommendation Draft, 5 June 2026; css-flexbox-1: Candidate Recommendation Draft, 14 October 2025; css-grid-2: Candidate Recommendation Draft, 26 March 2025; css-align-3: Working Draft, 30 January 2026; css-position-3: Working Draft, 7 October 2025; css-contain-2: Working Draft, 17 September 2022; css-conditional-5 TR: Working Draft, 30 October 2025; drafts.csswg.org/css-conditional-5/: its header reads W3C Working Draft, 30 June 2026; mediaqueries-4: Candidate Recommendation Draft, 19 February 2026; mediaqueries-5: Working Draft, 19 February 2026; css-logical-1: Working Draft, 4 December 2025; css-color-4: Candidate Recommendation Draft, 7 October 2026; css-color-5: Working Draft, 13 September 2026; css-transitions-1: Working Draft, 8 January 2026; css-transitions-2: Working Draft, 4 February 2026; css-animations-1: Working Draft, 2 March 2023. The TR header dates otherwise match the requested pin. Container queries use Conditional Rules 5; the obsolete Containment 3 material is excluded.
All requested MDN pages were opened. Observed Baseline banners: @layer and revert-layer widely available since March 2022; :is() and :where() since January 2021; :has() since December 2023; nesting selector since December 2023, with parts varying; CSSNestedDeclarations Baseline 2024, newly available since December 2024; subgrid widely available since September 2023; @container and container-type widely available since February 2023, with parts varying; container widely available since February 2023, with no asterisk in the fetched banner; @property Baseline 2024, newly available since July 2024; oklch(), oklab(), color() and color-mix() widely available since May 2023, with parts varying; light-dark() Baseline 2024, newly available since May 2024; @starting-style Baseline 2024, newly available since August 2024; transition-behavior Baseline 2024, newly available since August 2024, with parts varying; @scope Baseline 2026, newly available since March 2026; translate widely available since August 2022. The relative-colors and container-size-and-style-query guides have no Baseline banner. The web reader omitted dynamic compatibility-table cells, so the supplied relative-color 2024 and custom-property style-query 2026 support pins, including Safari's missing style-range syntax, were not independently table-verified. Those future-batch facts need a compatibility recheck before publication.
Contradictions and qualifications found: MDN Specificity models style attributes as 1-0-0-0 and says only !important overrides them; Cascade Introduction and Cascade 5 correctly place animations above normal style attributes and transitions above important declarations. Style attributes are element-attached cascade declarations, not selector weight. Specificity also calls order of appearance a proximity rule; this deck reserves scope proximity for @scope. MDN @layer broadly says unlayered styles always override layered styles, but its detailed precedence section and Cascade 5 correctly reverse that for important declarations. The revert-layer and all references suggest a rollback to another declaration in the current layer; Cascade 5 removes that layer's contribution and rolls back through lower-priority layers, then origins. The presentational-hint distinction between revert and revert-layer is excluded.
Cascade 6 section 2.5 says scope proximity wins regardless of specificity, contradicting its section 2.1 ordering and MDN @scope; specificity comes first. MDN @scope warns that & specificity varies by engine; those cards are excluded. The :where() reference's syntax block uses complex-selector-list, but its prose and Selectors 4 specify forgiving parsing. The Selectors 4 editor's draft confines forgiving lists to :is() and :where(); :has() takes an unforgiving relative-selector-list.
The BFC guide excludes overflow: clip in its list but overgeneralizes to overflow other than visible in an example; the overflow reference correctly excludes both visible and clip. The margin-collapsing guide's vertical wording generalizes to the block direction. The position reference's static z-index wording omits flex and grid items, and its nearest-positioned-ancestor summary omits transform-created containing blocks; the z-index reference and containing-block guide supply the qualifications. Automatic flex minimums have scrolling and sizing exceptions. The align-content reference now includes block containers; this deck tests its nowrap flex behavior. MDN lists query containers as stacking-context and BFC creators, and the container-queries guide still claims layout containment; the container-type reference and Conditional Rules 5 specify style plus size or inline-size containment and an independent formatting context. No card tests a query container's stacking context, BFC or fixed-position containing block. repeat() has no banner and conflicting fixed-size prose versus track-size generated grammar; established grid auto-repeat uses Grid 2's fixed-size restriction.
The registering-properties guide calls initial-value optional before correctly restricting omission to syntax '*'. It calls percentages computationally dependent despite its valid percentage example and the API specification's computation rules. Its registered-default summary, and similar API draft prose, omit the inherits:true case; the examples and normative rules use inherited or initial values as appropriate. The container-style-query guide incorrectly calls inherit and unset invalid for registered color properties; the API specification permits CSS-wide keywords. That guide also describes a 10em-to-30em example whose code uses 10em-to-20em. The media-query guide's blanket unknown-type-false wording omits negation: Media Queries 4 makes an unknown type false and its negation true. The length reference retains browser-choice wording for unprefixed viewport units but its explicit entries map them to large viewport units. The @keyframes last-same-name-rule summary omits layer precedence; layered name-collision cards are excluded. Relative-color channel keywords are numbers, and the current named-space two-color color-mix() forms are used. The requested behavior remains supported with these qualifications; the Snapshot's Display 3 classification and the blanket unknown-media-query wording require correction.

cards.statement: A normal declaration in a user style sheet overrides a normal author declaration on the same element.
cards.explanation: Normal author declarations outrank normal user declarations. The browser resolves origin precedence before it compares selectors.
cards.misconception: Normal user styles outrank normal author styles.

cards.statement: An important user-agent declaration outranks an important declaration in a user style sheet.
cards.explanation: Important declarations reverse the ordinary origin order, giving user-agent important declarations precedence over user important declarations.

cards.statement: A running CSS animation's value outranks a normal declaration in the element's style attribute.
cards.explanation: Animation values sit above normal author declarations in the cascade, including normal declarations attached through a style attribute.

cards.statement: An author declaration marked `!important` outranks the value supplied by an active CSS transition.
cards.explanation: During an active CSS transition, its generated value has higher cascade precedence than important declarations.
cards.misconception: Important declarations outrank active transition values.

cards.statement: A style attribute declaration outranks an author style rule when both have the same importance.
cards.explanation: The cascade gives element-attached declarations priority over author style rules of the same importance.

cards.statement: CSS inheritance passes the parent's used property value to its child.
cards.explanation: Inheritance transfers the parent's computed value. A used value includes later layout calculations.
cards.misconception: Inheritance transfers layout-resolved used values.

cards.statement: On the root element, `color: inherit` resolves to the property's initial value.
cards.explanation: The root has no parent from which to inherit. Explicit inheritance on the root therefore supplies the property's initial value.

cards.statement: An unspecified `border-style` on a child inherits its parent's border style.
cards.explanation: The border style does not inherit by default. An unspecified border-style uses its initial value, none.
cards.misconception: A parent's border style propagates to its children.

cards.statement: In ordinary block flow, `display: initial` restores the browser's `block` display for a `div`.
cards.explanation: The initial display value is inline. In ordinary flow, display: revert instead rolls back author styling and recovers the browser's block value for a div.
cards.misconception: initial restores element-specific browser stylesheet values.

cards.statement: `margin: inherit` makes a child use its parent's margin values.
cards.explanation: The inherit keyword explicitly requests inheritance for margin, a property whose default behavior is to use its own value.

cards.statement: `color: unset` selects the inherited color value for an element with a parent.
cards.explanation: The unset keyword follows the property's normal inheritance behavior. Color is an inherited property.

cards.statement: `all: initial` resets an element's unregistered custom properties to their initial values.
cards.explanation: The all shorthand leaves custom properties unchanged. It also excludes direction and unicode-bidi.
cards.misconception: The all shorthand includes custom properties.

cards.statement: Reopening a named `@layer` keeps the layer in the position established by its first appearance.
cards.explanation: A later block for an existing layer appends rules to that layer. Its position in the layer order stays fixed.

cards.statement: A normal ID rule in an earlier layer outranks a normal type rule in a later layer.
cards.explanation: For competing normal author declarations, the later layer wins before the browser considers selector specificity.
cards.misconception: An ID selector overcomes a lower-priority cascade layer.

cards.statement: Important author declarations in the first declared layer outrank those in later layers.
cards.explanation: The important flag reverses precedence among cascade layers, giving earlier layers priority for important declarations.

cards.statement: An unlayered important author declaration outranks a layered important author declaration.
cards.explanation: Within the author origin, important declarations in layers have precedence over important declarations outside layers.
cards.misconception: Unlayered declarations have highest priority even when important.

cards.statement: `revert-layer` restores an earlier declaration for the property in its current cascade layer.
cards.explanation: The revert-layer keyword removes its layer's contribution for the property and exposes lower-priority layers or the previous origin.
cards.misconception: revert-layer retries earlier declarations in the same layer.

source.title: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5: revert-layer

cards.statement: `@import "theme.css" layer(theme);` assigns the imported rules to the named theme layer.
cards.explanation: The layer() function on @import places the imported stylesheet's rules in the specified named cascade layer.

cards.statement: A top-level `@import` after an `@layer` block remains a valid stylesheet import.
cards.explanation: An @import after an @layer block is ignored. Layer statements, such as @layer theme;, are allowed before imports.
cards.misconception: The placement exception for layer statements also covers layer blocks.

cards.statement: `@scope (.card) to (.footer)` includes the matching scope-limit elements in its scope.
cards.explanation: An @scope lower boundary excludes the matched scope-limit elements and their descendants from the scope.
cards.misconception: The lower scope boundary includes its matched elements.

cards.statement: The bare `p` selector inside `@scope (#card)` keeps specificity 0-0-1.
cards.explanation: The scope-root selector sets the scope boundary rather than contributing to the specificity of a bare scoped selector.

cards.statement: An explicit `:scope` in a scoped selector adds 0-1-0 to selector specificity.
cards.explanation: The :scope pseudo-class contributes class-level weight when an author writes it explicitly in the selector.

cards.statement: Within one author layer, scope proximity takes precedence over selector specificity.
cards.explanation: The browser compares specificity before scope proximity. Proximity resolves competing declarations with equal specificity.
cards.misconception: A nearer scope root overcomes a more specific competing selector.

cards.statement: Inherited values from a scoped rule continue to descendants beyond its scope limit.
cards.explanation: Scope boundaries constrain selector matching. Inherited properties still pass values down the element tree beyond those boundaries.

cards.statement: The selector `[id="panel"]` contributes 0-1-0 to specificity.
cards.explanation: An attribute selector adds class-column weight even when the attribute being tested is id.

cards.statement: The `::before` pseudo-element adds weight to the CLASS column of specificity.
cards.explanation: A pseudo-element contributes to the TYPE column, with weight 0-0-1.
cards.misconception: Pseudo-elements carry the same specificity weight as ordinary pseudo-classes.

cards.statement: The universal selector `*` adds 0-0-1 to a selector's specificity.
cards.explanation: The universal selector contributes zero specificity, regardless of the elements it matches.
cards.misconception: Matching any element gives the universal selector type-column weight.

cards.statement: A child combinator `>` contributes zero weight to a selector's specificity.
cards.explanation: Combinators restrict relationships between matched elements, but add no weight to the specificity calculation.

cards.statement: One ID selector has greater specificity than a selector containing eleven classes.
cards.explanation: Specificity compares the ID column before the CLASS column. Counts in a later column do not carry into an earlier one.

cards.statement: `:is(.item, #panel)` has specificity 0-1-0 when the `.item` branch matches.
cards.explanation: The selector :is(.item, #panel) has specificity 1-0-0. The ID's weight applies even when .item is the matching branch.
cards.misconception: These selector functions use matching-branch specificity.

cards.statement: `:where(#panel .item)` contributes zero specificity despite the ID in its argument.
cards.explanation: The :where() function gives itself and its arguments zero specificity.

cards.statement: `:nth-child(2 of .item)` has the same specificity as `.item`.
cards.explanation: The selector :nth-child(2 of .item) has specificity 0-2-0: one pseudo-class weight plus the class weight from its of argument.
cards.misconception: The of selector replaces rather than adds to nth-child's own weight.

cards.statement: In `.card, #panel { & .title {} }`, `&` uses class-level weight when the parent matches `.card`.
cards.explanation: The nesting selector takes the greatest specificity in the parent selector list. Here the ID sets the weight of & to 1-0-0.
cards.misconception: The nesting selector uses the weight of the matching parent-list branch.

cards.statement: For normal unlayered author rules, a more specific selector wins over a later less specific selector.
cards.explanation: For competing declarations in that cascade group, the browser compares specificity before order of appearance.

cards.statement: Outside `@scope`, a closer ancestor in a selector increases that selector's specificity.
cards.explanation: The distance to an ancestor does not affect selector specificity. The selector components determine the weight.
cards.misconception: DOM distance contributes selector specificity.

cards.statement: A `p` color declaration beats a color inherited from a parent's ID rule.
cards.explanation: A declaration targeting the paragraph supplies its own color value. The parent's selector weight does not accompany an inherited value.

cards.statement: A `div`'s background color fills the margin area surrounding its border box.
cards.explanation: A box's background painting area stops at the outer border edge by default. Its margin lies outside that area.
cards.misconception: The margin area belongs to the element's background painting area.

source.title: Introduction to the CSS box model

cards.statement: `box-sizing: initial` makes `width` size the content box.
cards.explanation: The initial value of box-sizing is content-box, so the width applies to the content area.

cards.statement: With `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes the element's margins.
cards.explanation: Border-box sizing includes content, padding and borders in the specified width. Margins remain outside that width.
cards.misconception: Border-box sizing includes margins in width.

cards.statement: A child's `box-sizing` follows its parent's computed value through CSS inheritance.
cards.explanation: Box-sizing is a non-inherited property. A child's value comes from its own declarations or defaulting.
cards.misconception: Setting box-sizing on a parent propagates it to children.

cards.statement: A border-box content width stays at zero when padding and borders exceed the specified width.
cards.explanation: The browser floors the content width at zero. Padding and borders can make the resulting border box exceed the requested width.

cards.statement: Percentage `padding-top` uses the containing block's height as its reference.
cards.explanation: Percentage padding uses the containing block's inline size, which is its width in the assumed horizontal writing mode.
cards.misconception: Percentage top padding is relative to containing-block height.

cards.statement: Auto left and right margins center a fixed-width block in ordinary flow when horizontal space remains.
cards.explanation: The block layout algorithm distributes the remaining horizontal space equally between its two auto margins.

cards.statement: When `min-width` exceeds `max-width`, the minimum width wins.
cards.explanation: A conflicting maximum width does not force the used width below the specified minimum width.

cards.statement: A non-replaced box's preferred `aspect-ratio` influences sizing when at least one dimension is `auto`.
cards.explanation: The browser uses a preferred aspect ratio in automatic sizing. Two explicitly fixed dimensions leave it no automatic dimension to resolve.

cards.statement: `inline-size` controls a box's physical width in a vertical writing mode.
cards.explanation: In a vertical writing mode, inline-size maps to physical height because the inline axis runs vertically.
cards.misconception: inline-size maps to physical width regardless of writing mode.

cards.statement: With horizontal writing and RTL direction, `margin-inline-start` sets the right margin.
cards.explanation: The inline-start edge follows text direction. With right-to-left horizontal text, that edge is on the right.

source.title: Logical properties for margins, borders, and padding

cards.statement: With spare main-axis space, `justify-content: flex-start` aligns a `row-reverse` flex line at the left edge.
cards.explanation: In the assumed left-to-right writing direction, row-reverse puts main-start on the right. Flex-start aligns the items at that main-start edge.
cards.misconception: flex-start names a fixed physical left edge.

source.title: Aligning items in a flex container
